entries.question: Were Naaman and Ard the sons or the grandsons of Benjamin?
entries.summary: Genesis 46:21 lists Naaman and Ard as sons of Benjamin who migrated to Egypt. Numbers 26:40 lists Ard and Naaman as sons of Bela — making them Benjamin's grandsons, not his sons. Same names, different generational slots.
entries.commentary: The go-to apologist solution is telescoping: Archer and Kaiser both argue that Genesis 46:21 lumps descendants without strict generational markers and that Numbers 26 gives the more precise family tree. Possible, but it runs into the same problem we saw with Benjamin's age — if Benjamin was young enough in Genesis 44 to be called a "little one," the presence of ten sons and multiple grandsons at the migration becomes chronologically impossible. Friedman, Baden, and Carr place Genesis 46:8-27 in the Priestly tribal-list tradition and note that the Priestly census lists in Numbers are working from overlapping but not identical genealogical data. The Samaritan Pentateuch and LXX preserve variant readings in both passages that smooth some of the tension — another indication that ancient copyists were already trying to reconcile the lists and failing. Knoppers' work on Chronicles shows that the Chronicler's parallel list in 1 Chronicles 7:6-12 doesn't match either Genesis or Numbers cleanly, giving three distinct Benjaminite genealogies that disagree on generation counts and names. Three independent list-traditions, three incompatible family trees. The "telescoping" answer papers over a real data problem: the tribal censuses don't agree with each other, full stop.
entries.scholarship: Gary N. Knoppers, *I Chronicles 1-9* (AB; Doubleday, 2003). Joel S. Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch* (Yale, 2012). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

answers.answer: They were the sons of Benjamin
answers.answer_explanation:
And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi,
				    and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard. Genesis 46:21

answers.answer: They were the grandsons of Benjamin
answers.answer_explanation: And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman. Numbers 26:40

commentary_out.commentary:
Genesis 46:21 lists ten "sons of Benjamin" who went down to Egypt with Jacob: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. Numbers 26:40, in the wilderness census taken a generation or more later in the plains of Moab, places two of those names — Ard and Naaman — one rung lower on the family tree, listing them as "the sons of Bela" (Bela himself being Benjamin's firstborn in both rosters). On the Genesis reading the two men are Benjamin's sons; on the Numbers reading they are his grandsons through Bela. The names are identical and the relationship is incompatible.

The customary harmonization, argued by Archer and Walter Kaiser, is telescoping in reverse: Genesis 46:21 supposedly gathers Benjamin's wider household — sons and grandsons alike — under the loose clan-heading "sons of Benjamin," while Numbers 26 supplies the precise pedigree. The Hebrew בֵּן (ben) carries the burden, since it can denote a descendant generally rather than an immediate son, much as "the sons of Israel" names a whole nation. This is not impossible. The recurrence of the same names makes it plausible that the same individuals are in view, and "sons of Benjamin" can function as an eponymous header collecting later-attested family names under the founding ancestor. As a way of rendering Genesis and Numbers formally compatible, the move has genuine force.

Two problems weigh against treating the matter as cleanly resolved. First, the chronology strains. In the Joseph narrative Benjamin is repeatedly cast as the youngest son and as the *naʿar* ("lad"), the "little one" whose safety obsesses Jacob during the earlier journeys to Egypt (Genesis 43-44). Although the narrative spans years and Benjamin is no longer a small child by the descent in Genesis 46, the portrait of him as Jacob's tender, late-born favorite sits awkwardly with crediting him with ten sons — and, on the Numbers data, grandsons — at the migration. The friction is not that Benjamin must be an infant in chapter 46 but that the list's demographic depth pulls against the narrative's consistent characterization of him as the youngest, which is one reason critics read these rosters as schematic constructs rather than reportage.

Second, and more decisively, the Benjaminite genealogies do not merely disagree between Genesis and Numbers; they triangulate into incompatibility once the Chronicler is added — and, crucially, Chronicles is internally inconsistent with itself. 1 Chronicles 7:6 gives Benjamin three sons (Bela, Becher, Jediael), a roster matching neither Genesis nor Numbers in names or generation counts. But 1 Chronicles 8:1-2 then supplies a different set entirely (Bela, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, Rapha), so the divergence is not only between books but within a single book. There are thus at least three distinct Benjaminite list-traditions that cannot all be literally true together. It is fair to note that Numbers 26 is a clan census and 1 Chronicles 7-8 a multi-generational genealogy, so part of the divergence reflects differing genealogical scope; but the name discrepancy between 1 Chronicles 7:6 and 8:1 is not a matter of scope at all — it is two incompatible lists of Benjamin's own sons inside one composition.

Source and composition critics — Friedman, Baden, and Carr — locate Genesis 46:8-27 within the Priestly tribal-list tradition and observe that the Numbers 26 census, while related, draws on overlapping but non-identical data shaped to the needs of a military and inheritance census. The textual witnesses confirm that ancient readers already felt the friction: the Septuagint of Genesis 46:21 differs substantially from the Masoretic Text, redistributing the Benjaminite names across generations and even introducing grandsons in language drawn partly from Numbers 26, and the Samaritan Pentateuch preserves its own variant arrangement. Some scholars read these as harmonizing assimilation toward one another; whatever the precise intent, the variant readings show the lists were unstable and that scribes reworked them. Gary Knoppers's analysis of the Chronicler shows him reshaping received genealogies for theological and demographic purposes, not transcribing a fixed archive.

The telescoping defense can render Genesis and Numbers formally compatible by absorbing a generation into the elastic word "sons." But it does so by conceding that the tribal lists are schematic and divergent, and it cannot absorb the third, Chronicler tradition — discordant both with the Pentateuch and with itself — without admitting that the censuses do not fully agree.

Verdict: superficially harmonizable via telescoping, but the broader multi-source list tradition (Genesis, Numbers, and an internally inconsistent Chronicles) is genuinely discordant.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Genesis 46:21 can be read as listing Benjamin's wider household ('sons' = descendants), with Numbers 26:40 supplying the precise pedigree through Bela, so the same individuals occupy both lists; but this reconciles only two of at least three divergent Benjaminite genealogies, and 1 Chronicles disagrees both with the Pentateuch and internally (7:6 vs 8:1-2), so the underlying list-tradition remains genuinely discordant.

commentary_out.change_summary: Corrected the Knoppers Anchor Bible volume designation to AB 12 and added a Walter Kaiser (Hard Sayings of the Bible) citation to match the 'Archer and Kaiser' prose attribution, while retaining the three-tradition discordance analysis and partial harmonization.

issues.problem: The commentary asserts a sharp internal contradiction within Chronicles by contrasting 1 Chronicles 7:6 (Bela, Becher, Jediael) with 1 Chronicles 8:1-2 (Bela, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, Rapha) as 'two incompatible lists of Benjamin's own sons inside one composition,' and downplays the scope explanation specifically for this pair ('the name discrepancy ... is not a matter of scope at all'). This overstates the case: the relationship between 1 Chr 7:6ff. and 8:1ff. is genuinely debated, and many scholars do treat them as differing in source/scope/textual transmission (some even suspect 7:6-12 is partly a corrupted Zebulun/Dan list). Presenting the internal-contradiction reading as decisive ('more decisively') against the harmonization risks strawmanning, since defenders would dispute that 7:6 and 8:1 are simply parallel enumerations of identical scope.
issues.correction: Soften to acknowledge that the relationship of 1 Chr 7:6-12 and 8:1-40 is contested—some hold they reflect different sources/recensions or even a textually disturbed list—so that the internal divergence supports the broader 'discordant list-tradition' point without asserting it is indisputably two equivalent lists of Benjamin's immediate sons.

issues.problem: The claim that the LXX of Genesis 46:21 'redistributes the Benjaminite names across generations and even introduces grandsons in language drawn partly from Numbers 26' is correct in substance (LXX Gen 46:21 lists Benjamin's sons, then sons of Bela and grandsons, harmonizing toward Numbers), but the phrase 'drawn partly from Numbers 26' is an inference about the direction of harmonization that is not certain; it is hedged ('Some scholars read these as harmonizing assimilation'), so the risk is minor.
issues.correction: Retain the hedge; optionally state that the LXX plus reflects assimilation toward the Numbers 26 / 1 Chronicles structure without asserting the specific source borrowed.

entries.question: Who appeared to Moses in the burning bush?
entries.summary: Exodus 3:2 says "the angel of the LORD" appeared to Moses in the flame, and Acts 7:35 confirms it was an angel. But Exodus 3:4 in the same passage shifts and says "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush," and Mark 12:26 has Jesus himself affirm that God spoke to Moses at the bush. Same encounter, two different speakers.
entries.commentary: The traditional solution — endorsed by Calvin, carried by Kaiser, Walton, and Stuart — is that "the angel of Yahweh" is a functional stand-in for Yahweh himself throughout the Hebrew Bible, so "angel" and "God" can name the same being without contradiction. Some apologists go further and read the angel as a pre-incarnate Christophany. The pre-incarnate-Christ reading is a dogmatic overlay, not anything the text suggests. But even the broader "angel as God-surrogate" claim is doing heavy lifting. Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer have mapped the mal'akh YHWH formula across Hebrew Bible texts and shown it functions inconsistently — sometimes as Yahweh himself in disguise (Gen 16, Gen 22), sometimes as a genuinely separate emissary (Num 22, 2 Sam 24). In Exodus 3 the narrative oscillates: verse 2 has the angel appearing in the flame, verse 4 has Yahweh and Elohim both speaking. Friedman's source analysis splits the passage between J and E, each using different terms for the divine speaker. Carr, Baden, and Propp all treat the angel/God alternation in Exodus 3 as a redactor's seam rather than a unified theology — the E source tends to use "angel" or "God" circumlocutions while J uses "Yahweh" directly. The harmonization works at the level of mature second-temple theology (where "angel of Yahweh" got systematized as an avatar doctrine), but the Exodus 3 text itself preserves two source-strands with different names for who showed up at the bush.
entries.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, *The Early History of God* (Eerdmans, 2002). Benjamin D. Sommer, *The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel* (Cambridge, 2009). William H. C. Propp, *Exodus 1-18* (AB 2; Doubleday, 1999). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Douglas K. Stuart, NAC on Exod 3:1-6 (B&H, 2006).

answers.answer: God
answers.answer_explanation:
And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of 
				        the midst of the bush, and said, Moses, Moses. Exodus 3:4
				        
				        And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, 
				        I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? Mark 12:26

answers.answer: An angel
answers.answer_explanation:
And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, 
				        the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed. Exodus 3:2
				        
				        This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send [to be] a ruler and a deliverer 
				        by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush. Acts 7:35

commentary_out.commentary:
Within a few verses, Exodus 3 names two different beings at the burning bush. Verse 2 reports that "the angel of the LORD" (Hebrew malʾakh YHWH) appeared to Moses in the flame. Acts echoes this: 7:30 has "an angel" appear to Moses in the flame of fire in the bush, and 7:35 refers back to "the angel which appeared to him in the bush." But Exodus 3:4 says "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush" — with "the LORD" (YHWH) seeing and "God" (Elohim) calling in the same verse — and the ensuing self-revelation, "I am the God of Abraham" (3:6), is spoken in the divine first person; Jesus in Mark 12:26 attributes that speech directly to God. The same theophany is thus credited both to an angel and to God himself.

The classic harmonization, going back to Calvin and carried by Kaiser, Walton, and Stuart, is that the "angel of YHWH" functions throughout the Hebrew Bible as a manifestation or mouthpiece of YHWH himself, so that "angel" and "God" can denote one and the same presence without contradiction. There is real textual support. In Genesis 16 the angel of YHWH speaks as YHWH to Hagar, who then names YHWH "the God who sees me"; in Genesis 22 the angel of YHWH speaks in the first person as the one from whom Abraham did not withhold his son; and in Judges 6 Gideon, addressed by the angel of YHWH, concludes that he has seen God face to face. A subset of apologists presses further, identifying the angel as a pre-incarnate Christ (a Christophany). The Christophany reading is a dogmatic overlay with no warrant in the Exodus text itself, and even the milder "angel = God" identification, while genuinely attested, does heavy interpretive lifting.

The formula malʾakh YHWH is not consistent across the corpus. Mark S. Smith and Benjamin Sommer have shown that it sometimes denotes YHWH appearing in a created or quasi-human guise (Genesis 16, 22; Judges 6) and sometimes a genuinely distinct subordinate emissary (Numbers 22, where the angel obstructs Balaam; 2 Samuel 24, the destroying angel who is plainly not YHWH). The category is fluid, and reading every instance as "God himself" flattens that diversity. Sommer's work on divine "fluidity" in ancient Israel frames the angel as part of a wider pattern in which the deity's presence could be distributed into avatars — a conception later systematized but not yet doctrinally fixed in the Pentateuch.

Exodus 3 in particular bears the marks of composite authorship. Richard Friedman's source analysis, and the broader work of David Carr, Joel Baden, and William Propp, locate the burning-bush narrative at a seam between the J and E strands. Characteristically, E favors the more mediated language — "God" (Elohim) or "the angel of God" — as a way of distancing the deity from direct theophany, while J speaks of YHWH directly and anthropomorphically. The oscillation in Exodus 3 between "angel of YHWH" (v. 2), "YHWH" (v. 4a), and "Elohim" (v. 4b, 6) is, on this reading, the trace of a redactor splicing two accounts that named the divine speaker differently. The seam, not a unified angelology, produces the dual ascription. Propp notes that the angel of v. 2 effectively drops out of the narrative once God begins to speak, which is exactly what one expects if a later mediating layer (the angel) was prefixed to an older account of direct divine speech.

The New Testament data confirm that by the first century the bush-speaker could be named either way without anyone perceiving a problem. Luke, narrating Stephen's speech, twice says an angel appeared (Acts 7:30, 35), while Mark's Jesus says God spoke (Mark 12:26) — the same flexibility the canonical-theological harmonization describes, now embedded in the textual tradition itself.

So the harmonization works at the level of mature, post-biblical theology, where "the angel of YHWH" had been systematized as YHWH's manifest presence and where the New Testament writers could freely call the bush-speaker "God." At the level of the Exodus 3 text itself, however, the alternation is better explained as the merging of source-strands with different vocabularies for the divine than as a single coherent doctrine of self-manifestation. The two readings answer different questions: the canonical-theological one harmonizes the surface conflict, while the compositional one diagnoses a genuine diversity of underlying voices. Because the commentary's own analysis concedes that the source-critical reading leaves a real diagnostic difference behind the harmonized surface, this is best classed as partial rather than complete reconciliation.

Verdict: harmonizable within mature canonical theology (angel of YHWH as YHWH's manifest presence), but the alternation in Exodus 3 is best explained as a J/E source seam — partially harmonized.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: In the canonical/theological frame the 'angel of YHWH' (malʾakh YHWH) functions as YHWH's own manifest presence and mouthpiece (cf. Gen 16; 22; Judg 6), so 'angel' and 'God' name the same appearance without a factual conflict over who appeared; but the Exodus 3 alternation is better explained source-critically as a J/E seam, so a genuine diagnostic difference in the underlying material remains, making the reconciliation partial.

entries.question: Who gave the law to Moses?
entries.summary: The Exodus narrative (Exod 19:20, 20:22) has YHWH descending on Sinai and speaking the law directly to Moses — no intermediaries. But Galatians 3:19 explicitly says the law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator" — Paul is telling his Gentile converts that the Torah came through angels and a human mediator (Moses), not directly from God. Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2 echo the angel-mediation tradition. Two different models of Sinai revelation.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here actually has solid second-temple texture behind it, but it still leaves the contradiction largely intact. The argument: Exodus 19-20 says God descended on Sinai and spoke with Moses, but it doesn't explicitly deny angelic involvement. Second-temple Jewish tradition — Jubilees, Philo, Josephus, and the LXX translation of Deut 33:2 — developed a theology in which angels were present at Sinai and served as intermediaries in the law's transmission. Paul is drawing on this established tradition, not inventing it. Bruce (NICNT Galatians), Longenecker (WBC Galatians), and Moo (BECNT Galatians) all make this point, and Dunn's Galatians commentary goes further. On this reading, Galatians 3:19 isn't contradicting Exodus; it's drawing on a Jewish interpretive tradition that filled in Sinai with angelic mediators. That IS historically accurate. Philo's De Somniis and Josephus's Antiquities 15.136 both reference angelic involvement at Sinai. The LXX of Deuteronomy 33:2 reads "at his right hand were angels" where the Hebrew has "from his right hand was a fiery law." So Paul is working within an existing interpretive framework. Here's where the critical read lands. The Exodus narrative itself, in its plain reading, does NOT include angelic mediators. YHWH speaks, Moses hears, the people tremble and refuse direct revelation (20:18-21), and Moses becomes the mediator. But the mediator in Exodus is Moses, not angels plus Moses. The angelic-mediator tradition is a second-temple development, not an exegetical entailment of the Pentateuchal text. Paul in Galatians 3 is using this tradition for a specific polemical purpose — he's diminishing the Torah's ontological status to make room for Christ as a superior mediator. The more direct the law's origin, the harder for Paul to relativize it; the more layers of mediation (angels, then human mediator), the easier. Martyn in the AB Galatians commentary argues Paul is deliberately minimizing the law's divine directness. So Paul isn't just reporting a tradition; he's weaponizing it theologically. The contradiction between Exodus and Galatians is real, and the second-temple angelic-mediation tradition is interesting context but doesn't erase the difference in how Sinai is described.
entries.scholarship: J. Louis Martyn, AB 33A on Gal 3:19-20. James D. G. Dunn, *The Epistle to the Galatians*, BNTC (Hendrickson, 1993). Richard N. Longenecker, *Galatians*, WBC 41 (Word Books, 1990). Douglas J. Moo, *Galatians*, BECNT (Baker Academic, 2013). Hans Dieter Betz, *Galatians*, Hermeneia (Fortress Press, 1979). William H. C. Propp, AB 2A on Exod 19-20. Darrell D. Hannah, *Michael and Christ: Michael Traditions and Angel Christology in Early Christianity* (Mohr Siebeck, 1999).

answers.answer: Moses received the law directly from God.
answers.answer_explanation:
And the LORD came down upon mount Sinai, on the top of the mount: and the LORD called Moses up to the top of the mount; and Moses went up. . . . And the LORD said unto Moses, Thus thou shalt say unto the children of Israel, 
				        Ye have seen that I have talked with you from heaven. Exodus 19:20, 20:22

answers.answer: Angels gave the law to Moses through the hand of a mediator.
answers.answer_explanation:
Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; 
				        and it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Galatians 3:19

commentary_out.commentary:
Exodus and Galatians describe the giving of the law in different terms. The Sinai narrative in Exodus 19:20 and 20:22 has YHWH descend on the mountain, call Moses up, and declare, "Ye have seen that I have talked with you from heaven" — a direct, unmediated divine speech, with Moses as the human go-between (20:18-21). Galatians 3:19, by contrast, says the law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator" (diatageis di' angelōn en cheiri mesitou), and Acts 7:53 ("received the law by the disposition of angels") and Hebrews 2:2 ("the word spoken by angels") echo the same angelic-mediation tradition. The two accounts present different pictures of how Sinai's revelation reached Israel.

The harmonization has solid Second-Temple texture and is the strongest part of the apologetic case. Exodus 19-20 nowhere explicitly denies angelic participation, and a well-developed Jewish tradition by Paul's day populated Sinai with angels. The clearest evidence is the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 33:2, which in Rahlfs reads "at his right hand were angels with him" (ek dexiōn autou angeloi met' autou) where the Masoretic Hebrew has the obscure ʾesh dat ("a fiery law," or possibly "fire was a law"); the LXX text-form here is itself variable across witnesses, but it plainly introduces angels absent from the plain MT. Jubilees has the Angel of the Presence mediate the Sinai revelation and dictate the tablets to Moses (Jub. 1:27-2:1). Longenecker (WBC), Moo (BECNT), Betz (Hermeneia), and Dunn (BNTC) all observe that Paul is invoking an established interpretive framework rather than inventing one. (Josephus, Antiquities 15.136, is sometimes cited here for Herod's claim that the Jews learned their laws and the holiest of their ordinances "through angels" — the phrase is usually paraphrased rather than quoted, and the Greek angeloi in that passage is widely taken to mean human envoys or messengers, so its value as evidence for angelic mediation of the law is contested and considerably weaker than Jubilees or LXX Deut 33:2.) On this reading Galatians 3:19 is not denying Exodus but supplementing it from a tradition that filled in the heavenly retinue Exodus leaves implicit. That much is historically accurate and softens the apparent contradiction.

What the harmonization does not erase is that the plain sense of Exodus knows no angelic mediators of the law. In the narrative, YHWH speaks, the people tremble and beg not to hear the divine voice directly (20:18-19), and Moses alone becomes the mediator. The mediator in Exodus is Moses, not angels-plus-Moses; the angelic layer is a Second-Temple development, not an exegetical entailment of the Pentateuchal text. More important, Paul is not merely reporting the tradition — he is putting it to polemical work. Martyn (AB Galatians) argues that Paul deliberately minimizes the law's divine directness: the more layers of mediation between God and the law (angels, then a human mediator), the lower the law's ontological standing, and the more room for Christ as the superior and direct revelation. Galatians 3:20's cryptic remark that "a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one" pushes in the same direction, subordinating the mediated law to the unmediated promise given to Abraham. Betz reads the verse as part of Paul's argument that the law is provisional and inferior to the promise — a downgrade of Torah, not a neutral report.

The pliability of the tradition is itself telling. Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2 invoke the same angelic mediation to different rhetorical ends — Stephen to magnify Israel's guilt in disobeying a law so gloriously delivered, Hebrews to argue from lesser to greater (if the angel-mediated word was binding, how much more the word spoken through the Son). In none of these is angelic mediation treated as a diminishment except in Paul's hands. That Paul alone bends it downward shows the angelology is theologically loaded, chosen because it serves his argument against requiring Torah-observance of Gentile converts. Hannah's study of Michael and angel traditions documents how flexible and contested the Sinai-angelology remained in this period, and how readily it could be turned to opposite theological purposes.

Weighing it: the contradiction is not flat, because Exodus does not say "no angels were present" and Paul is drawing on a real interpretive tradition rather than fabricating one. To that extent the two can be held together. But they are not saying the same thing. Exodus portrays direct divine speech with Moses as the sole mediator; Galatians portrays a law ordained through angels and handed over by a mediator, deployed precisely to relativize that law. The difference is genuine, and it reflects developing Second-Temple theology and Paul's particular polemical needs rather than a single unified account of Sinai.

Verdict: partially harmonized — reconcilable through the angelic-mediation tradition, but a real difference in portrayal, sharpened by Paul's polemic, remains.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Galatians 3:19 draws on a genuine Second-Temple interpretive tradition of angelic presence at Sinai (LXX Deut 33:2; Jubilees 1:27-2:1), and Exodus 19-20 does not explicitly deny angelic involvement, so the accounts are not flatly contradictory; but Paul deploys that tradition polemically to diminish the law's directness, and Exodus's plain narrative knows only YHWH speaking with Moses as sole mediator, so a real difference in how Sinai is portrayed remains.

entries.question: How should the Canaanites be treated?
entries.summary: The Pentateuch and Joshua give four incompatible answers about what Israel was to do with the Canaanites. God promises to drive them out himself via hornets and an angel (Exodus 23, 33-34; Josh 3, 13, 23). Deuteronomy 7 and 20 command total extermination with no survivors. Numbers 33 says drive them out and destroy their cult sites. Ezekiel 47 envisions resident aliens inheriting land alongside Israel. These are not complementary policies — they are different programs.
entries.commentary:
This is a multi-answer contradiction and needs to be read structurally. The apologist response — from Copan, Flannagan, and Kitchen — is a layered harmonization. First, the herem (ban) commands are "ancient Near Eastern war rhetoric," exaggerated hyperbole not meant as literal extermination policy. Second, the drive-out passages describe the primary means, with violence only against those who resisted. Third, Ezekiel 47 is eschatological restoration, not Mosaic policy. On this reading the commands form a coherent, escalating program with literary hyperbole in the middle.

Let's take that steelman apart piece by piece. The "hyperbole" defense runs into Deut 20:16-17's explicit limiting clause: "save alive nothing that breatheth." That is the opposite of rhetorical hyperbole — it is a legal specification that narrows the application. Kitchen's ANE-parallels argument (Merneptah stele, Mesha stele) actually cuts the other way: those texts use identical herem language and describe actual atrocities, not literary flourishes. Lauren Monroe and Jacob Wright have demonstrated that ANE extermination rhetoric was understood as programmatic, not merely stylistic.

The source-critical explanation is cleaner. The drive-out tradition reflects older E and Priestly material assuming gradual dispossession (Exodus 23, 34). The extermination commands are Deuteronomistic, written centuries later during Josianic reform as ideological retrojection to justify cult purification (Deut 7, 20). Joshua 15-17 and Judges 1 already admit the program failed — Canaanites kept living there. Ezekiel 47 represents a late prophetic inclusivism that breaks entirely with the herem tradition. Baden, Friedman, Schmid, and Römer all treat these as literarily and historically distinct strata. There is no unified "Canaanite policy" — there are four policies from four periods stitched together by the final redactor. Apologetic harmonization requires treating the final form as a single voice, which is the one thing source criticism has shown it is not.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is a four-answer contradiction and must be read structurally. The Pentateuch and Joshua give incompatible programs for the Canaanites: (1) YHWH himself drives them out gradually by hornets and an angel, with Israel essentially passive (Exod 23:28-32; 33:2; 34:11; Josh 3:10; 13:6; 23:5); (2) Israel must exterminate them totally, leaving "nothing that breatheth alive" (Deut 7:1-2; 20:16-17); (3) Israel drives them out and destroys their cult installations (Num 33:51-53); and (4) resident aliens dwelling among Israel inherit land alongside the tribes as naturalized citizens (Ezek 47:22). These are not stages of one coherent plan; they assign different agents, different fates, and different statuses to the same population.

The most serious harmonization, advanced by Copan, Flannagan, and Kitchen, is layered. First, the herem ("ban") commands are ancient Near Eastern war rhetoric — hyperbole not meant as literal demography. Second, the drive-out texts describe the normal means, with killing reserved for those who resisted. Third, Ezekiel 47 is eschatological restoration, not Mosaic law. Assembled, this is meant to yield a single escalating program with stylized exaggeration in the middle.

Each plank is vulnerable. The hyperbole defense collides with Deuteronomy 20:16-17's explicit limiting clause: in the cities of the land "you shall save alive nothing that breathes." That is not a rhetorical flourish but a legal specification, set in deliberate contrast to the terms-of-peace rules for distant cities (20:10-15). Deuteronomy 20 establishes two warfare regimes — siege-with-tribute for far cities, total herem for the cities of the seven nations — and the contrast is the opposite of careless exaggeration; it is a juridical distinction. The ANE-parallels argument cuts against its own user: the Mesha (Moabite) Stele records Mesha devoting the inhabitants of Nebo to Ashtar-Chemosh using the cognate root ḥrm, and it describes an actual massacre of seven thousand, not a literary trope. Lauren Monroe and Jacob Wright have shown that such devotion-rhetoric was understood programmatically, as describing real cultic destruction, not mere bombast. The comparative evidence thus makes the herem texts more literal, not less.

Source and redaction criticism offers a cleaner account. The "driving out" tradition reflects older non-Priestly strata: the drive-out promises of Exodus 23:20-33 and 34:11-16 belong to the Covenant Code and the so-called cultic decalogue (J/E material), not to P, and they envision gradual dispossession over time — Exod 23:29-30 even explains the delay ("lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply"). The total-extermination commands are Deuteronomic, composed centuries later and framed by the ideology of cult centralization and purity; the herem rationale in Deut 7 and 20 is explicitly to prevent religious contamination ("lest they teach you to do after all their abominations," Deut 20:18), the central anxiety of the Josianic program. Joshua's own narrative oscillates and then concedes failure: Josh 15:63, 16:10, and 17:12-13, and especially Judges 1:19-36, repeatedly admit that the Canaanites were not driven out but reduced to forced labor and continued to dwell in the land. Ezekiel 47:22, finally, represents a late prophetic inclusivism that grants the gēr a permanent landed inheritance "as born in the country" — a complete reversal of the herem. Friedman, Baden, and Römer treat these as literarily and historically distinct layers; Konrad Schmid's work on the formation of the Pentateuch (Genesis and the Moses Story; and the Gertz/Levinson/Rom/Schmid volume) likewise locates the conquest materials in separate compositional horizons. John Collins frames the resulting diversity as one of the clearest internal tensions in the canon.

No single Mosaic policy is recoverable; the final text stitches four programs from four periods. The harmonization succeeds only by treating the redacted whole as one authorial voice — the very assumption source criticism has dismantled. Even granting some hyperbole in conquest summaries, hyperbole cannot convert an explicit legal command to exterminate into a command merely to expel, nor can it reconcile expulsion with naturalized inheritance. Daniel Block, treating Ezek 47:21-23, notes how startling the inclusion of resident aliens as landed heirs is against the background of the conquest traditions; it is not an extension of the earlier program but a deliberate departure from it. The programs differ in agent (God vs. Israel), in fate (death vs. expulsion vs. coexistence), and in status (annihilated enemy vs. landholding citizen).

Verdict: a genuine contradiction reflecting compositional layering, not a coherent escalating policy.

entries.question: Is it OK to drink alcohol?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Lamentations, Hosea, Amos, Habakkuk, Matthew, John, Romans, Galatians, Ephesians
entries.summary: The Bible's stance on alcohol is not a spectrum — it is a pile of mutually inconsistent positions. Some texts positively command drinking: wine as covenant blessing (Gen 27:28), festival wine (Deut 14:26), God commanding joyful drinking (Eccl 9:7). Others forbid it absolutely for Nazirites, priests on duty, prophets, and nursing mothers of promised sons (Num 6, Lev 10:9, Isa 28:7, Judg 13). Proverbs 20-23 issues strong warnings, while Song of Solomon and the wedding at Cana endorse it enthusiastically. What the Bible actually contains is every possible position at once.
entries.commentary:
This is a twelve-answer structural contradiction and it needs to be engaged as what it is — the SAB has catalogued the Bible's full internal diversity on drinking, and a single harmonization has to somehow absorb all of it. Apologists from Kaiser to Köstenberger try the standard contextualization move: each passage speaks to a specific situation. Nazirites and priests-on-duty have role-specific prohibitions. Proverbs warns against drunkenness not drinking. Deut 14:26 is festival context. Jesus' wine at Cana was "new wine," practically non-alcoholic. On this reading the Bible teaches moderation with role-specific abstention and there is no contradiction at all.

That harmonization is the only game in town for conservative exegesis, and parts of it have real force — the moderation vs. drunkenness distinction in Proverbs is exegetically solid. The "new wine was basically grape juice" claim is just wrong. Robert Stein's work in *Christianity Today* and the broader scholarship on oinos and yayin confirm that ancient wine was fermented, alcoholic, and intoxicating. Deut 14:26 explicitly authorizes using tithe money for shekar — "strong drink" — and commanding you to drink before YHWH. That is not moderation language. That is festival consumption.

The Habakkuk 2:16 citation in the SAB list is mis-framed — it is actually an imprecatory curse against Babylon ("thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered"), not a command to drink. Same with Lamentations 4:21 — that is sarcasm against Edom. So the SAB's "get drunk and naked" answers are misreadings of prophetic judgment rhetoric. Those two answers should probably be revised.

What remains is still a real tension. The priestly abstention (Lev 10:9) sits inside a cult where wine libations are commanded at the sanctuary (Num 15:5, 28:7). The Nazirite vow treats wine as defiling while the covenant blessing framework treats it as a gift. Prophetic texts alternate. The clean answer is that biblical materials come from diverse traditions and social locations — priestly, wisdom, prophetic, festival — with different evaluations of wine. Judges 13, the Samson birth narrative, is a good case: the angelic command for Samson's mother to abstain is a Nazirite-extension trope specific to the birth narrative genre, not general ethics.

Verdict: the real contradiction here is not within any single tradition but across the biblical canon as a whole. Moderation-plus-role-exception is a viable harmonization for the commands; the prophetic curses against drunkenness coexist with the Torah's festival drinking mandates, and no amount of context-carving erases that.

commentary_out.commentary:
The Skeptic's Annotated Bible assembles a wide catalogue and presents it as a pile of mutually exclusive positions. Sorting by genre, context, and original language shows that most of the material coheres around a moderation-plus-role-exception ethic, while a genuine residual tension remains, and two of the listed prooftexts are simply misread.

First the misreadings. Habakkuk 2:16 ("drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered") is not a command to drink; it is an imprecatory taunt within the woe-oracles against Babylon (2:15-16), reversing onto the oppressor the cup of staggering it forced on others. Lamentations 4:21 ("Rejoice ... O daughter of Edom ... thou shalt be drunken, and shalt make thyself naked") is bitter sarcasm announcing Edom's coming humiliation. Both belong to the genre of prophetic judgment, where the "cup" is a stock metaphor for divine wrath (cf. Isa 51:17; Jer 25:15-29). Reading them as endorsements of drunkenness mistakes the rhetorical force; these two SAB answers should be revised or dropped.

Second, a popular apologetic claim must also be rejected: that the wine Jesus made at Cana, or the wine the texts commend, was unfermented grape juice. The lexical evidence is against it, though it needs to be stated carefully. Hebrew yayin and Greek oinos denote fermented, intoxicating wine; the Cana steward's remark that hosts serve the good wine first "and when men have well drunk (methysthōsin), then the worse" (John 2:10) presupposes inebriating wine. Hebrew tirosh, usually rendered "new wine" or must, is a different and contested case: lexicography (e.g. HALOT) commonly treats it as the freshly pressed product whose degree of fermentation is debated, and it is frequently distinguished from yayin precisely on that ground. Yet tirosh is not simply innocent grape juice either — Hosea 4:11 pairs "wine and new wine" (yayin and tirosh) as together "taking away the heart," attributing an intoxicating effect to it. Robert Stein's survey of wine in New Testament times documents that ancient wine, though often diluted, was genuinely alcoholic. Deuteronomy 14:26 settles the question for the Torah: tithe-money may be spent "for whatsoever your soul desires ... for wine, or for strong drink (shekar)" and consumed in rejoicing before YHWH. Shekar specifically denotes a strongly intoxicating beverage, so this is a positive festival mandate, not mere tolerance — Christensen reads it as authorizing celebratory consumption at the central sanctuary.

With those clarified, the bulk of the catalogue harmonizes by context. The prohibitions are role-specific and temporary. The Nazirite vow (Num 6:1-3) brackets wine for the duration of a consecration, and the mother of Samson abstains as a Nazirite-birth extension (Judg 13:3-4) — Daniel Block notes this belongs to the birth-annunciation type-scene, not general ethics. Priests abstain only while on duty in the tent (Lev 10:9, in the immediate aftermath of Nadab and Abihu), even though wine libations are commanded at the sanctuary (Num 15:5; 28:7); Milgrom reads the priestly ban as a sobriety requirement for cultic discernment, not a general prohibition. Isaiah 28:7 condemns priests and prophets who err through drink — an abuse, not a categorical ban. The Proverbs cluster (20:1; 23:20-21, 29-35) and the NT vice-lists (Eph 5:18; Gal 5:21; Rom 13:13) target drunkenness, not consumption; Van Leeuwen notes the wisdom tradition's careful distinction between the gift of wine and the folly of the "winebibber." Romans 14:21 is situational abstention for the sake of a weaker conscience.

Against these stand the positive evaluations: wine as covenant blessing (Gen 27:28), wisdom's feast (Prov 9:5), and the divine command to "eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a merry heart" (Eccl 9:7). The Song of Songs likewise celebrates wine in an erotic-domestic register ("thy love is better than wine," Song 1:2; cf. 5:1), which Athalya Brenner analyzes as part of the poem's sensory food-and-drink imagery; Köstenberger and Bauckham read Cana as deliberately affirming the goodness of wine within celebration. Even the prophetic woes that the SAB enlists under "don't do it" mostly indict excess and oppression rather than drinking as such: Amos 6:1-6, for instance, condemns the complacent elite "that drink wine in bowls" — its target is luxurious, callous overindulgence by those "at ease in Zion," not the moderate use of wine commended elsewhere. Hosea 4:11 ("wine and new wine take away the heart") is a proverbial warning against intoxication's effect on judgment, again an abuse-critique.

What survives all this contextualization is a real but narrower tension within the canon's social locations: the priestly and Nazirite ideal treats wine as something to be set aside for holiness, while the festival law of Deuteronomy and the wisdom and celebration traditions treat it as a divine gift to be enjoyed. These reflect different streams — priestly, wisdom, prophetic, festival — with differing evaluations, and no single rule fully reconciles abstention-as-holiness with drink-as-blessing. The materials come from diverse traditions and social settings, and the canon preserves all of them side by side without homogenizing them.

Verdict: largely harmonizable by genre and role, with two SAB prooftexts (Hab 2:16; Lam 4:21) misframed as commands, but a genuine residual tension between priestly/Nazirite abstention and the Torah's positive festival drinking mandate remains.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Most of the cited texts resolve by context: role-specific abstention (Nazirites, priests on duty, the Nazirite-birth mother), warnings against drunkenness and luxurious excess rather than drinking in Proverbs and the prophets (e.g. Amos 6:1-6), and festival/celebration endorsement elsewhere. Two SAB 'commands to drink' (Hab 2:16; Lam 4:21) are misread judgment oracles and should be set aside. A real residual tension remains, however, between the priestly/Nazirite abstention ideal and the Torah's positive festival drinking mandate (Deut 14:26), so the harmonization is only partial.
